description: Discourage broad process killing: pkill/killall by name, SIGKILL as a first resort, and pgrep -f or an unread PID lookup used to decide or to signal.

no-pkill.message: Do not kill by name (pkill, killall): it can match your own shell or an innocent process. To find a process, run `pgrep -xl <name>` as its own command, read the PID, confirm it is the right process, then `kill <pid>`.

messages.text: Do not kill by command-line pattern (pkill -f): it can match your own shell and unrelated processes. List the candidates as its own command, with a bracket in the pattern so it cannot match its own text (`pgrep -fl '[v]ite --port 5173'`), read the PID and the command line, confirm it is the right process, then `kill <pid>`.
messages.messageShort: No pkill -f. List with `pgrep -fl '[x]pattern'` alone, confirm the PID, then `kill <pid>`.

kill-9.message: SIGKILL gives the process no chance to clean up (temp files, locks, child processes). Send SIGTERM first (`kill <pid>`) and escalate only if it does not exit.

no-pgrep-status.description: Never use the exit status of an unguarded pgrep -f (&&, ||, !, if, while, until).
no-pgrep-status.message: Do not use pgrep's exit status in &&, ||, ! or if: with -f it can match your own shell and never turns false. Run `pgrep -fl '[x]pattern'` (or `pgrep -xl <name>`) as its own command and read the output. To wait for a process to exit, poll `kill -0 <pid>` with a PID you already identified.
no-pgrep-status.messageShort: No pgrep exit status in conditions. Poll `kill -0 <pid>`.

messages.text: Do not wait on a process by looping on pgrep: with -f it can match your own shell and the loop never ends. Get the PID once with `pgrep -fl '[x]pattern'` as its own command, then wait with `while kill -0 <pid> 2>/dev/null; do sleep 5; done` (or watch it from a Monitor).
messages.messageShort: No pgrep in a wait loop. Get the PID once (`pgrep -fl '[x]pattern'`), then poll `kill -0 <pid>`.

no-unchecked-pid-lookup.description: Never act on a PID lookup (pgrep, ps, pidof, lsof) that is piped or captured instead of read first.
no-unchecked-pid-lookup.message: Do not pipe or capture a PID lookup (head, wc, tr, echo "$(...)"): with -f it can include your own shell, so lists and counts are off by one. Run it as its own command and read the output; for the newest or oldest PID use `pgrep -n` / `-o`. Put a bracket in the pattern (`'[x]pattern'`) so it cannot match itself.
no-unchecked-pid-lookup.messageShort: No piped or captured PID lookups. Run it alone; `pgrep -n` / `-o` for the newest or oldest PID.

messages.text: Do not feed a PID lookup straight into kill or xargs kill: you would signal whatever it matched, possibly your own shell. Run the lookup as its own command (`pgrep -fl '[x]pattern'` or `pgrep -xl <name>`), confirm the PID, then `kill <pid>`.
messages.messageShort: No lookup straight into kill. Run it alone, confirm the PID, then `kill <pid>`.

warn-pgrep-in-loop.description: pgrep inside a loop or under watch: fine for reading, not for deciding.
warn-pgrep-in-loop.message: pgrep inside a loop or under `watch`: make sure you only read its output. Do not loop on it to wait for a process or to choose what to signal. To wait for a process to exit, poll `kill -0 <pid>` with a PID you already identified.
warn-pgrep-in-loop.messageShort: pgrep in a loop or `watch`: read only. Poll `kill -0 <pid>` to wait.

warn-pgrep-full-cmdline.description: pgrep -f matches full command lines, including your own shell.
warn-pgrep-full-cmdline.message: `pgrep -f` matches full command lines, including your own shell's, so its output can list your shell. For a known process name use `pgrep -xl <name>`. For a command-line pattern bracket it, `pgrep -fl '[v]ite --port 5173'`, and do not spell the unbracketed text anywhere else in the same command (it would match your shell again).
warn-pgrep-full-cmdline.messageShort: `pgrep -f` can list your own shell. Use `-xl <name>` or bracket the pattern: `'[v]ite'`.

incident.description: Actively firefighting; the user accepts broad process killing
